You actually don't need radar, and ATC can do non-radar "procedural" control where they block off sections of airways or entire airports, one-in one-out at a time, like sections of railroad track. There are still a few parts of the remote US, as well as large sections of Northern Canada, where radar coverage is nonexistant and ATC is done via procedural control. Radar outages also happen on occasion, which would necessitate this. As for lack of radio, this would only work if ATC blocked out your entire route from start to finish - which isn't practically ever done. Otherwise, they need to be able to maintain positive control over your flight since the airspace isn't reserved, which means conflicts are possible. If you lose radio communication, it's an emergency and they'll move everyone out of your way. This doesn't work very well if everyone loses radio communication simultaneously.

This can be partially solved by always allowing pasting of content copied from the same OS process, but multi-process applications would still face hurdles. Another variation of that is scripting. I have various scripts and CLI aliases that take the current clipboard contents and do something with it. Show HN: Jevmem – Auto Tracked Project Rules for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor hi HN, I'm AJ. Have been using Claude Code every day, and I was done re-typing the same project rules in every new chat. So I built this. We try to follow some rules in our coding projects. For eg: "we use pnpm, not npm". The problem is, i tell claude about this rule in one chat, when i start another chat, i have to retype it. Also, when my team opens the same repo using another ai tool lets say cursor, they dont see the rule in their chat. Not cool. So I built jevmem. It saves your project's rules in a file in your repo. and before Claude Code runs a command, it checks the command against those rules. How it works: 1) You chat with Claude Code like normal. 2) jevmem saves your rules, decisions and everything that failed, one line each, in a file called JEVMEM.md in your repo. 3) You commit JEVMEM.md like any other file. 4) Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can all read it. now, your team also gets it when they pull. for example: on Mon you tell Claude "we use pnpm, not npm". On Tuesday your teammate pulls and opens the repo in Cursor. They can see the pnpm rule. oh and guard is my favourite part. So before Claude Code runs a command or edits a file, jevmem checks it against your rules. If it may break one of your rules, Claude Code stops and asks you first. Eg: your rule is "don't hand-edit db/migrations/, those files are generated". 3weeks later, in a new session if claude tries to edit a migration, Claude Code stops and shows: jevmem: this may break a saved rule: "Don't hand-edit db/migrations/: those files are generated." (JEVMEM.md) You can also retrieve failed attempt. Like if you tried caching API responses in memory, and it broke the build, claude will remember that and some time later when you do the same thing, Claude tells you "Already tried: ..." with the reason. Numbers from our tests: -> Claude broke a project rule and left it in the code: 0 of 15 sessions with jevmem, 9 of 15 without it. We checked each one by hand. -> Claude followed decisions made earlier in the project: 66 of 72 sessions with jevmem, 28 of 72 without. Tbh, a CLAUDE.md file that you keep updating yourself did about as well here (67 of 72). The difference is that jevmem updates the file for you, likewise for cursor and codex. jevmem also works alongside Claude Code's own auto memory. It doesn't replace it. The catches: - The guard works in Claude Code only. - You need a paid TypeSafe API key. jevmem's requests are billed to that key. - Your message text is sent to TypeSafe to be scored. Common secrets are removed first. - Nothing stored remotely. You turn it on per project. - We ran the tests on our own test projects. (MIT license) Full results: https://avinash-jetwani.github.io/jevmem/results/ Install: 1. In claude: Plugins > Discover > jevmem > Add 2. npm install -g jevmem 3. In your project folder: jevmem setup Repo: https://github.com/Avinash-jetwani/jevmem I'd like to hear about your genuine feedback and how we could make it better!

> Essentially all of our problems are caused by excessive population Except they aren't. This is the old Malthusian claim and it has been debunked time and again. > Wars Historically, war has been on a downward trajectory for a long time, certainly when measured by the violence and death any given person is likely to experience. Most war is not about the scarcity of resources. It is usually about power, the desire to dominate others, greed, and other intangibles, and of course defending oneself from such actors. > migration Like war, this claim is reducible to the one about limited resources, because "overpopulation" (whatever that means) per se is not a cause of anything. People generally migrate because somewhere else looks better in some way, usually because the destination is economically better developed and have better institutions. This has nothing to do with absolute resources, but with the standard of living in their home country relative to the standard elsewhere. Refugees and so on are a very small percentage of any global migration. > resource depletion This claim begins with a current understanding of the available resources. What we have found instead is that with more people, we have more resourcefulness and discovery. Farming is an excellent example. Innovation in agriculture tracks population growth. Today, we have more food than any of our ancestors would have dreamed of. We waste enormous amounts of food. > hunger, water scarcity Famine is nonexistent in the developed world and almost completely absent everywhere else. Most hunger is a matter of resource misallocation, not because there isn't enough to go around. > we can finally see a way to a possible future without scarcity This misunderstands scarcity, as if it were some fixed piece of pie on the table before us. According to this simplistic understanding, yeah, sure, you'll have to slice up that pie into thinner and thinner pieces until eventually everyone gets close to nothing. But this is not how things work. In practice, the more people there are, the more labor and ingenuity there is that scales non-linearly (including those caused by agglomeration effects and specialization). People will not only find new pies, but they will find things other than pies, or ways to replenish the supply in a renewable way. > The economic engine will never be more powerful than it is now Bold claim. History does not support it. Population contraction doesn't have to last forever and we can't know how economies will unfold. > where growth isn't purely consumptive I will say here that consumerism is a real problem, because it is not only wasteful in a number of ways, but it entrenches a habit of thinking that consumption is the purpose of life rather than a means to support it. Look at where the most consumption and waste occurs and you'll find it doesn't align with population density as a simplistic account of human beings would suggest. What population contraction might achieve in the interim is that it may force a course correction. People are very stubborn and easily attached to bad habits, to the point that entire economic and political orders are reshaped and become dependent on those bad habits to function, entering into a vicious cycle that entrenches these very habits and bakes them into a common cultural sensibility of what is normative. We have refused to wean ourselves off the drug of consumerism, which I claim is one of the primary, fundamental, and underlying ideological and cultural causes and drivers of population contraction because the imperatives of consumption conflict with having children. As a result, we suffer the self-destructive consequences, and these consequences may very well force us into abandoning consumerism because it will have been made impossible to sustain. Time will tell.

This is an ETTUS B210 attached to a dual 4090 box. It's a polyphase channelizer that takes the entire airband, channelizes it using cuda code on GPU, demodulates it, detects transmissions, throws away data tx and then feeds the tx through a voice model I created for transcription. That felt completely unacceptable, and I set out to create a radio that could monitor everything in real-time, all the time, and alert on emergencies. That has extended to transcribing and creating situational awareness for a chunk of airspace. I'm an IFR pilot. I fly a T206H regularly in IMC around here and I'm a ground instructor. The 2009 deficit was high because of the 2008-2010 financial crisis. Deficits increase dramatically in economic downturns because tax collections decline (job losses, lower profits, bankruptcies) and increased spending (unemployment, bailouts). Most mainstream economists think it's good for a government to increase deficit spending temporarily during a recession because it helps prevent deeper recessions that cause long-term impairment of the tax base. If you let half the auto industry fail, for example, it may take a long time for your tax base to recover and start generating taxable income again. After the crisis, there was bipartisan agreement that the deficit needed to be reduced, but the disagreement was on how. Obama was willing to cut spending but also wanted to increase taxes on higher income households, while the Republicans in Congress drew a hard line against any tax increases and wanted deeper spending cuts. In the end, they reached bipartisan bills, including the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012. The debt ceiling brinksmanship was political theater. Republicans used the threat of defaulting on US debt in order to extract concessions from Democrats without having to agree to any policy demands. Congress passed laws with required spending every year and no one has the legal authority to not spend it. If Congress really cared about reducing the deficit, they wouldn't pass spending bills that required deficit spending. As for increasing debt in the 2010s, I think it was viewed as a potential long-term problem but sustainable because interest rates were quite low. When inflation was at 2% and interest is at 2%, the US government was able to borrow money at 0% in real terms. Government spending on roads, airports, and even marginally productive projects that increase economic growth could be viewed as rational.
